summary.text: The Roman Republic was the era of classical Roman civilisation from the overthrow of the Roman Kingdom, traditionally dated to 509 BC, until the Roman Empire was established in 27 BC.
During this period, Rome's control grew from the city's immediate surroundings to hegemony over the entire Mediterranean world.
Its government used annual magistracies overseen by a senate, but it was an elective oligarchy, with a number of powerful families largely monopolising the senior magistracies.

facts.label: Start and end
facts.value: From the overthrow of the kings to the Empire in 27 BC

facts.label: Greatest rival
facts.value: Carthage, against which Rome waged three wars

facts.label: Plebs gain equality
facts.value: Political equality achieved by the 4th century BC

facts.label: Defeat of Carthage
facts.value: Rome won at the Battle of Zama in 202 BC

items.prompt: Rome elected its magistrates each year, yet a handful of powerful families held most senior offices. What kind of system fits this?

options.label: A direct democracy
An elective oligarchy
A hereditary monarchy
A military dictatorship

items.explain: There were annual elections, but powerful families monopolised the senior magistracies, so it was an elective oligarchy, not a true democracy.

items.prompt: A closed elite held office while a far more numerous group of commoners had little say. How did that struggle between the two orders end?

options.label: Peacefully, with the commoners winning political equality
By a civil war that destroyed the elite
With the elite exiling the commoners' leaders
With the commoners kept out of office until the Empire

items.explain: The Conflict of the Orders was resolved peacefully, with the plebs achieving political equality.

items.prompt: The late Republic saw political violence at home. Combined with that violence, what led to the civil wars that broke the Republic?

options.label: A conquest of the city by a foreign army
A popular revolt that restored the monarchy
Powerful generals who acted with great independence
The loss of the war against Carthage

items.explain: Political violence at home together with powerful semi-autonomous generals led to civil wars that broke the Republic.

items.prompt: Why do many historians point to the Senate giving Octavian the title Augustus?

options.label: It marks Rome's final victory over Carthage
It marks the founding of the Republic itself
It marks the murder of Julius Caesar
It is often seen as marking the Republic's end and the Empire's start

items.explain: Octavian's receipt of the title Augustus from the Senate is often seen to mark the end of the Republic and the beginning of the Empire.

items.prompt: A historian contrasts the peaceful Pax Romana of the Empire with the Republic that came before. What was the Republic's condition?

options.label: Near-constant war
A long peace broken by a few civil wars
Peace kept by the Senate's standing army
War fought only against Carthage

items.explain: Unlike the Pax Romana of the Empire, republican Rome was in a state of near-perpetual war.

items.prompt: The Gauls sacked Rome around 387 BC. How did Rome's fortunes go after that?

options.label: It stayed a small city for generations afterward
It conquered most of Italy within a century and became a great power
It fell under Carthaginian rule for a time
It gave up the Republic and chose a monarch again

items.explain: After the Gallic sack, Rome conquered most of the Italian peninsula in a century and became one of the Mediterranean great powers.
